clue.text: 8's new version of a Roman Pict, ca. 1740

definitions.note: 8-across is Hogarth, and the clue points to one of his paintings

indicators.note: a new version of the following words means their letters are rearranged into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A dated note about a reworking of an ancient Roman figure of a Pict from around 1740.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new version of' rearranges A ROMAN PICT CA. Hogarth (8-across) painted his portrait of Captain Thomas Coram, founder of London's Foundling Hospital, in 1740, which the closing date confirms.
explanation.definitionFit: Hogarth's celebrated full-length portrait of the Foundling Hospital's founder is known by its sitter's name and rank.

clue.text: Firm information on church has convincing power

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company, a firm
GEN is British slang for information
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A company holding facts about a church is persuasive.
explanation.definitionFit: Cogence is the quality of being forceful and persuasive in argument.

clue.text: Faultless, like le Carré' spy

explanation.surface: A spy in a le Carré novel is without flaw.
explanation.walkthrough: John le Carré's 1986 novel is titled A Perfect Spy; the clue as printed drops the s of Carré's.
explanation.definitionFit: Faultless means flawless; and le Carré's spy novel names its spy with this adjective.

clue.text: Followers more certain than Reed's?

parts.note: followers who stick fast, unlike a reed shaken by the wind, which bends every way

explanation.surface: Disciples who are steadier than those of someone named Reed.
explanation.walkthrough: The reed is the biblical 'reed shaken with the wind', a byword for wavering; those who cling firmly are steadier than that.
explanation.definitionFit: Supporters of a cause cling to it, as the Latin root 'stick to' suggests.

clue.text: Scene of Herzog's highest endeavour Idle Thoughts of an Idle Fellow in the Russian novel?

parts.note: Maurice Herzog led the 1950 French expedition that first climbed Annapurna, in the Himalaya

explanation.surface: The setting for a mountaineer's loftiest achievement.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue as held repeats 5-down's clue after its own words; only the first part belongs here. Annapurna, which Herzog climbed, is in this Himalayan kingdom.
explanation.definitionFit: Annapurna, the first eight-thousand-metre peak climbed, stands in this Himalayan country.

clue.text: Idle Thoughts of an Idle Fellow in the Russian novel?

definitions.text: Idle Thoughts of an Idle Fellow in the Russian novel?

parts.words: Idle Thoughts of an Idle Fellow in the Russian novel?
parts.note: borrows Jerome K. Jerome's book title to describe the famously lazy hero of Goncharov's Russian novel

explanation.surface: Jerome K. Jerome's essay collection recast as a Russian novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Goncharov's 1859 novel's hero spends most of it lying in bed; Idle Thoughts of an Idle Fellow is a Jerome K. Jerome title.
explanation.definitionFit: Goncharov's title character is literature's archetype of idleness, the novel named after him.

clue.text: Pedestal in archeologist's macro-terminology

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the run of letters of the archaeologist's long word

explanation.surface: A plinth mentioned in an archaeologist's grand technical jargon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points inside 'macro-terminology'.
explanation.definitionFit: An acroter is a plinth or pedestal for a statue at the apex or corner of a pediment.

clue.text: The short cut of 26 in 1957?

parts.note: points to a one-act play written in 1957 by the barrister-playwright of 26-across, about a cheap, quick legal brief

explanation.surface: A quick route taken by a certain writer in 1957.
explanation.walkthrough: 26 is John Mortimer, whose 1957 radio play concerns a brief handed to any barrister in court for a nominal fee, a short cut to representation.
explanation.definitionFit: A brief taken by a barrister from a prisoner in the dock for a token fee, and Mortimer's play of that name.

clue.text: Engraver has small house with courtyard

parts.note: HO is the abbreviation for house
a garth is an enclosed yard or cloister garden

explanation.surface: An artist lives in a little home with a yard.
explanation.walkthrough: William Hogarth was famous for his engraved series such as A Rake's Progress.
explanation.definitionFit: William Hogarth made his name with satirical prints from his own engraved plates.

clue.text: Mark causing indentation, if not a break, on leaf

definitions.text: Mark causing indentation, if not a break, on leaf

parts.words: Mark causing indentation, if not a break, on leaf
parts.note: describes the printer's sign that starts a new paragraph on a page, shown by indenting or by a line break

explanation.surface: A blemish that dents a leaf, if it does not snap it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaf' is a page, not foliage; the mark is the reversed-P paragraph sign.
explanation.definitionFit: The pilcrow is the paragraph sign, marking where a new paragraph begins.

clue.text: Latin Werther, perhaps, from Franz Xaver

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the words could take another form, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Latin version of Goethe's Werther, maybe, by a man named Franz Xaver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges LATIN WERTHER. Franz Xaver Winterhalter was a German court portrait painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Xaver is the forename of the nineteenth-century German royal portraitist.

clue.text: Nijinsky was a noble one

parts.note: the ballet term for a male principal of princely roles is this French word followed by 'noble'

explanation.surface: A remark that the great Russian dancer was an aristocrat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'noble' is not about rank: a male lead in classical princely roles is called a danseur noble.
explanation.definitionFit: Male ballet dancer, the French word used in the phrase for a lead in classical roles.

clue.text: Joe in the attic?

parts.note: an attic is a room at the top, the title of John Braine's novel whose hero is called Joe

explanation.surface: Someone named Joe hiding in the loft.
explanation.walkthrough: John Braine's Room at the Top follows Joe Lampton; an attic is literally a room at the top.
explanation.definitionFit: Joe's surname in Braine's novel, whose title names a room under the roof.

clue.text: Scott-Moncrieff's was sweet

parts.note: Scott-Moncrieff titled his translation of a Proust volume Sweet ... Gone, with this word in the gap

explanation.surface: A remark that the translator's something was sugary.
explanation.walkthrough: C. K. Scott-Moncrieff rendered Proust's Albertine disparue as The Sweet Cheat Gone.
explanation.definitionFit: A swindler; Scott-Moncrieff's Proust title calls Albertine a sweet one.

clue.text: Poem on choker, perhaps, can be read by a clergyman

definitions.text: can be read by a clergyman

indicators.note: in an across entry one piece set on another comes after it

parts.note: a choker is worn round the neck, so it stands for the place it goes
a verse is a poem

explanation.surface: A poem about a necklace that a priest could recite.
explanation.walkthrough: The neck verse was the Latin psalm a condemned man read to claim benefit of clergy and escape hanging, saving his neck.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin passage, usually Psalm 51, that an accused read to prove he was a cleric and escape the gallows.

clue.text: Happy to include what is fashionable by Jim Crace

indicators.note: the first word takes the second inside it, holding it within

parts.note: content means happy
IN means fashionable

explanation.surface: Pleased to take in the latest trend from a novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to include' is the container signal; 'what is fashionable' is the usual crossword IN. Continent (1986) was Jim Crace's first book, so 'by Jim Crace' defines it as a title.
explanation.definitionFit: Jim Crace's debut book of linked stories bears this title.

clue.text: Suspiciously fast Canadian dramatist?

parts.note: the Canadian sprinter stripped of 1988 Olympic gold for doping shares the name, give or take an h, of a Jacobean playwright

explanation.surface: A Canadian playwright who is surprisingly quick.
explanation.walkthrough: Ben Johnson, a Canadian sprinter, was disqualified for drug use in 1988; the dramatist's name drops the h.
explanation.definitionFit: The author of Volpone, whose name nearly matches a doping sprinter's.

clue.text: Work of fiction to behold from actor/dramatist

parts.note: a novel is a work of fiction
lo is an old word meaning look or behold

explanation.surface: A book to look at by a stage writer and performer.
explanation.walkthrough: Ivor Novello was a Welsh actor, composer and playwright.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivor Novello wrote and starred in his own musical plays.

clue.text: "I am always of the with the learned if they speak first" (William Congreve)

definitions.text: "I am always of the with the learned if they speak first" (William Congreve)

parts.words: "I am always of the with the learned if they speak first" (William Congreve)
parts.note: a quotation from Congreve with one word missing after 'of the', which the solver supplies

explanation.surface: A line from Restoration comedy about agreeing with clever people.
explanation.walkthrough: The line, from Congreve's Incognita, reads 'of the same ...'; the clue as printed loses the word 'same' before the gap, which the solver must fill.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word in Congreve's line is a noun for a view or belief.

clue.text: Letter for England in sacred river

indicators.note: the abbreviation sits inside the river's name

parts.note: Alph is the sacred river in Coleridge's Kubla Khan

explanation.surface: A message on behalf of England in a holy river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts E inside ALPH, the river of Coleridge's Kubla Khan.
explanation.definitionFit: The first character of the Hebrew alphabet.

clue.text: Lack of belief in Otway protagonist

definitions.text: Lack of belief in Otway protagonist

parts.words: Lack of belief in Otway protagonist
parts.note: Thomas Otway wrote a comedy called The Atheist, whose title figure lacks belief in God

explanation.surface: A Restoration hero turns out to be faithless.
explanation.walkthrough: Otway's 1683 comedy The Atheist names its leading character by his creed, or lack of one.
explanation.definitionFit: Disbelief in any god.

clue.text: Captivate man (roué possibly)

indicators.note: possibly signals the letters could be ordered another way

explanation.surface: A rake is perhaps able to charm a man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges MAN ROUE.
explanation.definitionFit: To charm someone into falling in love.

clue.text: Sound off rail

explanation.surface: A noise coming from a railing.
explanation.definitionFit: To sound off and to rail both mean to protest loudly against something.

clue.text: Transatlantic greeting from J. G. Ballard ssing: "So sweet love that April morn" (Bridges)

definitions.text: Transatlantic greeting from J. G. Ballard

parts.words: Transatlantic greeting from J. G. Ballard
parts.note: Ballard's 1981 novel set in a future United States is titled with this salutation plus America

explanation.surface: A friendly word sent across the ocean by a British novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue as held runs into a garbled line from Bridges ('So sweet love seemed that April morn'); only the first part belongs here. Ballard wrote Hello America.
explanation.definitionFit: The everyday salutation begins Ballard's novel title Hello America.

clue.text: Emil has reformed as Melville narrator

indicators.note: reformed means the letters are formed again in a new order

explanation.surface: A man named Emil has changed his ways and become a novelist's storyteller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reformed' rearranges EMIL HAS. 'Call me Ishmael' opens Moby-Dick.
explanation.definitionFit: The narrator of Moby-Dick introduces himself in its famous first line.

clue.text: "God —s himself in many ways " (Tennyson)

parts.note: a line from Tennyson's Morte d'Arthur with the verb missing, to be supplied

explanation.surface: A Tennyson line about divine providence.
explanation.walkthrough: From The Passing of Arthur: 'And God fulfils himself in many ways'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb means carries out or brings to completion.

clue.text: Poem on minced pies is quite an event in book

indicators.note: in an across entry the piece on another follows it
minced means chopped up, so the letters are cut and mixed

parts.note: an ode is a poem

explanation.surface: A poem about mince pies is a real happening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'minced' is the anagram signal, apt beside pies; 'on' places the poem after them in an across entry. An episode is one incident in a longer story.
explanation.definitionFit: An incident within a longer narrative, as a part of a story.

clue.text: Barrister shows Australian policeman leading regicide

indicators.note: one piece leading means it comes before the other

parts.note: a john, short for John Hop, rhyming slang for cop, is Australian slang for a policeman
Roger Mortimer engineered the murder of Edward II

explanation.surface: A lawyer exhibits an Aussie cop at the head of a king-killer.
explanation.walkthrough: John Mortimer was a barrister as well as the writer of Rumpole of the Bailey.
explanation.definitionFit: John Mortimer practised at the Bar before and during his writing career.
